The two error outputs carry the real failure: the `errno` of the syscall that failed and its `strerror` text. Both may be passed undeclared, as in PHP — the call defines them as `int` and `string`. A failed open also raises PHP's `Unable to connect to <address> (<reason>)` Warning, whether or not the error outputs were passed; `@` suppresses it. A host that does not resolve reports php-src's own `php_network_getaddresses: getaddrinfo for <host> failed: <reason>` text — that failure has no `errno`, so `&$error_code` stays `0` — and warns twice, as PHP does. | 389:Socket addresses use `[tcp://]host:port`, `udp://host:port`, `unix:///path`, or 390:`udg:///path`.
